sections.title: Mental model — from steps to Big-O

blocks.md: L1 counted steps honestly. Interviews compress that into **Big-O**: how running cost *grows* as input grows, ignoring constants and small-input noise. `3n + 500` steps and plain `n` steps are both **O(n)** — same growth *shape*.

items: **O(n²) / O(2ⁿ) / O(n!)** nested pairs / subsets / orderings — escape these early

blocks.label: read complexity off code shape
blocks.py:
# single pass over n            -> O(n)
for i in range(n): pass

# two independent passes         -> O(2n) = O(n)
for i in range(n): pass
for j in range(n): pass

# nested dependent loop          -> O(n^2)
for i in range(n):
    for j in range(i + 1): pass

# halving                        -> O(log n)
i = n
while i > 1: i //= 2

items.q: Complexity of visiting every cell of an n×n matrix?
items.explain: n rows × n columns = n·n operations.

items.q: Why is O(2n) reported as O(n)?
items.explain: Doubling every entry doesn't change the curve family.

blocks.md: **A pointer stores an address. A reference is an alias. Both touch data without copying it.**

blocks.label: three ways to hand over data
blocks.py:
# Python passes object REFERENCES; ints are immutable so rebinding
# never affects caller - closest mental model to by-value.
def by_value(x): x = 99

# mutable containers DO propagate changes (alias behavior):
def mutate(lst): lst.append(99)     # caller sees it!

# Interview mapping: C++ const& ~ passing tuple/str freely (immutable),
# out-slots ~ returning tuples instead of reference args.

blocks.md: **Interview reflex:** big inputs go by `const&` (`const vector<int>& v`) — read access, zero copy. Output slots go by `&`. Raw pointers are for walking structures or optional values.
Raw arrays forget their length when passed (they decay to pointers). **`vector`** is the interview-default container: knows its size, grows on demand, O(1) indexing.

blocks.md: **I solve ONE part, recursion handles the rest — plus a base case that stops the world.**
Two mandatory parts: (1) **base case** — smallest input answered directly; (2) **recursive step** shrinking toward it. Each call lives on the **call stack** — pause points stacking like plates.

blocks.md: **Default copying copies MEMBERS as-is — two objects end up sharing one resource. Deep copy builds a second resource so each object owns its own.**

blocks.label: deep copy constructor
blocks.py:
# Python has no manual copy ctor; use copy module semantics:
import copy
shallow = copy.copy(src)      # top-level only, inner refs shared
deep = copy.deepcopy(src)     # fully independent clone

# Class owning resources implements __copy__ / __deepcopy__
# (Rule-of-Three equivalent).

blocks.text: static · const · inline · friend in one breath

items: **static member** — belongs to the CLASS, shared by every object (one box for all buildings)
**static function** — callable without any object; cannot touch non-static members
**const member function** — promises not to modify the object: `int get() const`
**inline** — hint to paste small function bodies at call site (saves call overhead, grows binary)
**friend** — grants an outside function/class access to private members (use sparingly)

sections.title: Maths machinery — Euclid, Sieve, Fast Power

blocks.md: `gcd(a,b) = gcd(b, a%b)` — repeatedly replace the pair until the second hits 0. The survivor is the answer.

blocks.label: gcd + lcm formula

blocks.text: Sieve of Eratosthenes — all primes < n in O(n log log n)

blocks.label: sieve (optimized inner start)
blocks.py:
sieve = [True] * (n + 1)
sieve[0] = sieve[1] = False
i = 2
while i * i <= n:
    if sieve[i]:
        for j in range(i * i, n + 1, i):   # start at i*i!
            sieve[j] = False
    i += 1

blocks.md: Two classic optimizations hiding here: inner loop may start at `i*i` (smaller multiples were already marked by smaller primes) and outer loop stops at `sqrt(n)`.

blocks.title: Trace: sieve marking up to 30 (primes found: 2,3,5,7,...)

blocks.text: Binary exponentiation — pow in O(log b)

blocks.label: fast power, iterative
blocks.py:
def bin_pow(base, exp):
    result = 1
    while exp > 0:
        if exp & 1:                 # odd bit -> multiply in
            result *= base
        base *= base                # square the base
        exp >>= 1                   # consume the bit
    return result

items.q: Why start sieve marking at i*i?
options: smaller multiples already marked by smaller primes
items.explain: Any k·i with k<i was handled during prime k's pass.

items.q: binPow computes x¹³ with how many multiplications (roughly)?
items.explain: 13 = 1101₂ → 4 squarings + up to 4 multiplies ≈ exponent's bit count.

options: a/gcd*b stays in range where a*b might overflow
items.explain: Overflow discipline starts now — a recurring interview theme.

sections.title: Problem set — L2 ladder (two stacked skills each)

items.title: Alphabet Palindrome Pattern
items.statement: Row r prints A,B,C… rising then falling back ('ABA' style). Derive char offset from column position vs row length.
hints: Chars are numbers: 'A' + k.
Rising part: col<=r uses col-1 offset; mirror the falling half.
Formula first, code second.

solutionCode.label: chars are numbers: rise to A+r-1, then mirror back
solutionCode.py:
def alphabet_pyramid(n: int) -> str:
    rows = []
    for r in range(1, n + 1):
        rising = ''.join(chr(ord('A') + c - 1) for c in range(1, r + 1))
        falling = ''.join(chr(ord('A') + c - 1) for c in range(r - 1, 0, -1))
        rows.append(rising + falling)        # peak is not repeated
    return '\n'.join(rows) + '\n'

items.complexity: Time O(n²) characters emitted. Space O(n²) for the returned string.

followups.q: Why does the falling loop start at r − 1 and not r?
followups.a: Starting at r would print the peak letter twice — row 3 would read ABCCBA instead of ABCBA. The peak belongs to the rising half only; the mirror begins one step back.

followups.q: What is `'A' + c - 1` doing?
followups.a: Characters are integer codes, so adding an offset to 'A' walks the alphabet. Column 1 must map to 'A', hence the −1. Deriving the offset from the column index first, then coding, is the habit this exercise is training.

items.title: Number of 1 Bits
items.statement: Count set bits in an unsigned integer.
hints: n & 1 reads last bit; n >>= 1 drops it.
Bonus: Brian Kernighan n &= (n-1) clears lowest set bit per step — loop runs popcount times.

solutionCode.label: Brian Kernighan: clear the lowest set bit each pass

items.complexity: Naive O(number of bits) = O(32). Kernighan O(popcount) — as many iterations as there are set bits. Space O(1).

followups.q: Why does n & (n−1) clear the lowest set bit?
followups.a: Subtracting 1 flips the lowest set bit to 0 and turns every zero below it into 1. ANDing with the original keeps only the bits above that position, so exactly one set bit disappears per step — which is why the loop runs popcount times, not 32.

followups.q: When is the naive shift loop preferable?
followups.a: When you need the bits themselves rather than just the count — for example printing the binary representation, or testing a specific position. Kernighan destroys positional information as it goes.

items.title: Power of Two
items.statement: Return true if n is a power of 2, O(1) preferred.
hints: Powers of two have exactly ONE set bit.
n & (n-1) deletes a set bit — zero left means single-bit number.
Watch n=0.

solutionCode.label: exactly one set bit
solutionCode.py:
def is_power_of_two(n: int) -> bool:
    return n > 0 and (n & (n - 1)) == 0   # n > 0 guard is essential

followups.q: What goes wrong without the n > 0 guard?
followups.a: n = 0 gives 0 & -1 == 0, so it would wrongly report true. Negative numbers in two’s complement can also pass — e.g. the most negative value has a single set bit. The guard is not defensive padding; it is load-bearing.

followups.q: How would you test for a power of four?
followups.a: It must be a power of two AND have its single bit in an even position. Mask with 0x55555555 (bits 0, 2, 4, …): `n > 0 && (n & (n-1)) == 0 && (n & 0x55555555) != 0`.

items.title: Count Primes
items.statement: Count primes strictly below n using sieve, not trial division.
hints: Sieve to n, sum true flags.
Inner start i*i, outer bound i*i<=n.

solutionCode.label: Sieve of Eratosthenes, marking from i*i

items.complexity: Time O(n log log n) for the sieve. Space O(n) for the flag array.

followups.q: Why can the inner loop start at i², not 2i?
followups.a: Every composite k·i with k < i already carries a smaller prime factor and was struck out during an earlier pass. The first multiple of i that no smaller prime has touched is i·i. This is what turns the sieve from O(n log n) into O(n log log n).

followups.q: When is trial division still the better choice?
followups.a: For a single primality test, or when n is huge and you cannot afford an O(n) array. The sieve pays off only when you need many primes below a fixed bound — it trades memory for amortised speed.

items.title: Pow(x, n)
items.statement: Implement pow with negative exponents and n can reach ±2³¹ — overflow trap included.
hints: Handle negative exp: invert base, exponent becomes positive.
Casting INT_MIN to positive overflows — use long long (or long long abs).

solutionCode.label: binary exponentiation, exponent widened to avoid overflow
solutionCode.py:
def my_pow(x: float, n: int) -> float:
    e = n
    if e < 0:
        x, e = 1 / x, -e
    result = 1.0
    while e > 0:
        if e & 1:            # this bit of the exponent is set
            result *= x
        x *= x               # square the base for the next bit
        e >>= 1
    return result

items.complexity: Time O(log n) — the exponent halves each step. Space O(1) iterative.

followups.q: Where exactly is the overflow trap?
followups.a: n can be INT_MIN = −2^31, whose negation is not representable as a 32-bit int. Writing `n = -n` on an int is undefined behaviour. Copying into a 64-bit variable before negating is the fix — this is the trap the problem is built around.

followups.q: Why is this O(log n) rather than O(n)?
followups.a: Each iteration consumes one bit of the exponent, and an exponent up to 2^31 has 31 bits. You multiply at most twice per bit, so roughly 60 multiplications replace two billion.

items.title: GCD (Euclid, both orders)
items.statement: Iterative AND recursive versions; prove to yourself order of arguments doesn't matter.
hints: If a<b, first modulo swaps them automatically.
Recursive: gcd(a,b)=b==0?a:gcd(b,a%b).

solutionCode.label: Euclid, both forms

items.complexity: Time O(log min(a,b)). Space O(1) iterative, O(log) stack for the recursion.

followups.q: Does argument order matter?
followups.a: No. If a < b then a % b == a, so the first step swaps them and costs one extra iteration. The algorithm self-corrects — worth stating out loud rather than adding a defensive swap.

followups.q: What is gcd(0, 0) and gcd(n, 0)?
followups.a: gcd(n, 0) = n, since every integer divides 0. gcd(0, 0) is conventionally 0 — this code returns it naturally because the loop never runs. Mention it as the degenerate case rather than being caught out by it.

items.title: LCM and GCD together
items.statement: Return both; remember a·b = gcd·lcm and the divide-first trick.
hints: Compute gcd first.
lcm = a/g*b with long long.

solutionCode.label: divide before multiplying so the product never overflows

items.complexity: Time O(log min(a,b)), dominated by the gcd. Space O(1).

followups.q: Why divide before multiplying?
followups.a: a·b can overflow 64 bits even when the lcm itself fits comfortably. Since g always divides a, `a/g` is exact and the intermediate stays small. It is the same value by associativity, but only one ordering is safe.

followups.q: Does a·b = gcd·lcm hold for negatives?
followups.a: Only up to sign. gcd and lcm are conventionally non-negative, so take absolute values first — which is what this code does — otherwise you can produce a negative "lcm".

items.title: K-th Bit Set or Not
items.statement: Check whether bit at position k (0-indexed) is set.
hints: Mask: 1<<k isolates position k.

solutionCode.label: isolate position k with a shifted mask
solutionCode.py:
def is_kth_bit_set(n: int, k: int) -> bool:
    return (n & (1 << k)) != 0

followups.q: Why `1LL << k` rather than `1 << k` in C++?
followups.a: The literal 1 is an int, so shifting it by 32 or more is undefined behaviour — it may return garbage rather than 0. Promoting to long long first makes shifts up to 63 well-defined. Python has arbitrary-precision integers and no such limit.

followups.q: How would you set or clear bit k instead of reading it?
followups.a: Set: `n | (1LL << k)`. Clear: `n & ~(1LL << k)`. Toggle: `n ^ (1LL << k)`. All three build on the same isolating mask.

items.title: Add Two Numbers as Arrays
items.statement: Digits of two huge numbers given as arrays; output their sum's digits.
hints: Walk from least significant end.
carry = sum/10, digit = sum%10 — school addition formalized.
Don't forget trailing carry.

solutionCode.label: school addition from the least significant end

items.complexity: Time O(max(n, m)). Space O(max(n, m) + 1) for the result.

followups.q: Why is `carry` part of the loop condition?
followups.a: The final carry can create a new leading digit — 999 + 1 needs four digits from three-digit inputs. Ending the loop when both arrays are exhausted would silently drop it. Testing all three conditions handles the growth without a special case afterwards.

followups.q: How does this change for linked lists stored least-significant-first?
followups.a: It gets simpler — you traverse forward and append as you go, so no final reversal is needed. That is LeetCode 2, and the storage order is precisely why it is considered easier than the array form.

items.title: Factorial of Large Number
items.statement: 100! has 158 digits — store digits in an array/vector, multiply digit-by-digit.
hints: Keep digits reversed in storage.
Per multiplier: carry = temp/10 propagates across cells.
Grow array while carry remains.

solutionCode.label: digits stored least-significant-first, multiply cell by cell
solutionCode.py:
def big_factorial(n: int) -> list[int]:
    d = [1]                          # stores 1, least significant first
    for m in range(2, n + 1):
        carry = 0
        for i in range(len(d)):
            temp = d[i] * m + carry
            d[i] = temp % 10
            carry = temp // 10
        while carry:                 # grow while the carry survives
            d.append(carry % 10)
            carry //= 10
    return d                         # reverse to print

items.complexity: Time O(n × digits) ≈ O(n² log n). Space O(digits) — 100! has 158 digits.

followups.q: Why store the digits reversed?
followups.a: Growth happens at the most significant end. With least-significant-first storage that is a push_back at the tail — O(1). Storing them in reading order would require inserting at the front on every carry overflow, which is O(n) each time.

followups.q: Why can the carry exceed 9 here, unlike in F012?
followups.a: F012 adds two digits plus a carry, so the maximum is 19 and the carry is at most 1. Here a digit is multiplied by m, which can be 100, so temp reaches ~900 and the carry needs its own draining loop rather than a single push.

revisionCard: Big-O = growth shape; constants dropped; nested loops multiply, sequential loops add
const& for big inputs · & for outputs · * for structures/optional
Recursion mantra: solve one part + shrink + base case; depth costs stack
Init list REQUIRED for const/reference members; Rule of Three when class owns raw resource
static = one-per-class · const method = promise not to modify · friend = controlled privacy bypass
Sieve: mark from i², stop outer at sqrt — O(n log log n)
binPow: square base, consume exponent bits — O(log b)

glossary.def: Upper-bound growth shape of cost versus input size; constants ignored.
Rare expensive ops spread across many cheap ones average to constant per op (vector growth).
Raw arrays passed to functions lose size info, becoming pointers.
LIFO region holding paused function frames; recursion depth lives here.
Directly-answerable smallest input that terminates recursion.
Own a raw resource? Write destructor + copy ctor + copy assignment yourself.
Constructor syntax initializing members BEFORE body; mandatory for const/ref members.
Mark composites by crossing multiples of each prime; precomputes primality for a whole range.
Square-and-multiply using exponent's bits — log-time powers.
Sort predicate must be a strict weak ordering (comp(a,a)==false) or sort corrupts memory.
